questions.text: Which sentence uses a semicolon CORRECTLY?
options: I love swimming; and running on the beach.
The rain finally stopped; we ran outside to play.
She was tired; because she had run all the way home.
He grabbed his bag; his keys; and his phone.
questions.expectedAnswer: The rain finally stopped; we ran outside to play.
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 'The rain finally stopped; we ran outside to play.'

Here's why:
A semicolon joins two CLOSELY RELATED INDEPENDENT CLAUSES (each could stand alone as its own sentence). Both 'The rain finally stopped' and 'we ran outside to play' are complete sentences on their own.
You should NOT put a conjunction (and, but, because) after a semicolon — that's why option 1 ('; and') and option 3 ('; because') are wrong.
A semicolon is also not used to separate items in a simple list — option 4 should use commas.
Exam tip: a useful test — could you replace the semicolon with a full stop and have two grammatically correct sentences? If yes, the semicolon is probably correct.

questions.text: The character is angry. Which sentence is the BEST example of 'show, don't tell' AND ALSO uses sensory imagery?
options: She was very angry about what had happened in the kitchen.
She felt angry and upset deep inside her chest.
Her jaw clenched, and the door slammed shut behind her with a crack that rattled the cups on the shelf.
She told her mother she was extremely angry and walked away.
questions.expectedAnswer: Her jaw clenched, and the door slammed shut behind her with a crack that rattled the cups on the shelf.
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the option about the clenched jaw and slamming door.

Here's why:
'Show, don't tell' means the writer reveals an emotion through ACTIONS, BODY LANGUAGE and SENSORY DETAIL instead of stating it directly.
This sentence shows anger through a physical action (jaw clenching, slamming door) AND uses sensory imagery (the SOUND of the crack and the cups rattling).
The other options either tell the reader directly ('She was very angry') or show the action without the sensory detail.
Exam tip: at merit level, look for answers that achieve TWO things at once — not just the obvious one.

questions.text:
Rewrite this sentence to make it more descriptive and engaging. Your new version must:
• be one or two sentences long
• use AT LEAST TWO different language features (e.g. simile, metaphor, personification, sensory imagery)
• keep the original meaning (a dog moving across a field).

Original sentence: 'The dog ran across the field.'
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for each language feature that is used effectively (max 2). Both must be identifiable.

1 mark may be deducted if the rewrite changes the basic meaning, contains errors, or only adds adjectives without using techniques.

Examples of strong rewrites:

'The golden retriever exploded across the sun-bleached paddock like a streak of liquid sunshine, his ears flapping in rhythm with the wind.' (Simile + sensory imagery + personification of the wind.)

'Tongue lolling, the scruffy terrier zigzagged through the tall summer grass, nose twitching at every invisible scent the breeze carried.' (Sensory imagery + personification + listing for rhythm.)

Do NOT award full marks for rewrites that simply add adjectives ('the big brown dog ran fast') without recognisable techniques.

questions.text:
Read these two sentences:

(A) 'The sunset was very beautiful.'
(B) 'Ribbons of coral and gold bled across the horizon as the sun melted into the sea.'

Sentence B is more effective for TWO reasons. Which row identifies BOTH reasons?
options: Sentence B uses metaphor ('bled', 'melted') and visual imagery ('ribbons of coral and gold'), letting the reader picture the scene rather than just being told it is beautiful
Sentence B is longer and uses more difficult vocabulary
Sentence B uses bigger adjectives and more punctuation
Sentence B contains a rhetorical question
questions.expectedAnswer: Sentence B uses metaphor ('bled', 'melted') and visual imagery ('ribbons of coral and gold'), letting the reader picture the scene rather than just being told it is beautiful
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the metaphor + imagery option.

Here's why:
Length alone does not make writing better. What makes sentence B effective is its FIGURATIVE LANGUAGE.
'Bled' and 'melted' are metaphors that personify the sun and sky, while 'ribbons of coral and gold' is visual imagery that creates a clear, vivid picture.
Sentence A simply tells the reader 'it was beautiful' without showing.
Exam tip: 'show, don't tell' applies just as much to landscapes as to characters.

questions.text:
Write the OPENING PARAGRAPH (4–6 sentences) of a narrative set at a school sports day. Your writing must:
• establish a clear MOOD or atmosphere (e.g. excitement, nervousness, chaos, anticipation)
• use AT LEAST TWO different language features (e.g. simile, metaphor, personification, sensory imagery, short sentences for impact)
• include sensory details from at least THREE senses (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste)
• introduce a single MAIN CHARACTER (named or referred to) whose feelings the reader can sense.
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks total. Award one mark for each of the following criteria when clearly met:

1 mark — Clear, sustained mood (the whole paragraph stays in one atmosphere — excitement, nerves, chaos, anticipation, etc.).

1 mark — At least TWO identifiable language features used effectively (not forced) AND sensory details from at least THREE senses.

1 mark — A main character is introduced whose feelings the reader can sense, and the paragraph shows control of sentence variety (e.g. a short punchy sentence among longer ones).

Excellence responses will weave all the criteria together naturally rather than ticking them off, and will use specific NZ details (e.g. 'the smell of cut grass and sunscreen', 'the school field at lunchtime', 'the starter's whistle') where natural.

Do NOT award full marks if the paragraph reads as a list of features ('I will use a simile. The track was like...') rather than a coherent piece of writing.

questions.text:
Write a SHORT PERSUASIVE PARAGRAPH (5–8 sentences) arguing EITHER that schools should start later (e.g. 10 a.m. instead of 9 a.m.) OR that mobile phones should be banned in classrooms during lessons. Your writing MUST:
• state your position clearly in the FIRST sentence
• use AT LEAST THREE different persuasive techniques from this list: a statistic or fact, a rhetorical question, emotive language, expert opinion, repetition, direct address ('you'), an anecdote
• use at least ONE piece of supporting evidence (it can be invented but must sound plausible)
• end with a strong CALL TO ACTION.
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks total. Award one mark for each criterion when met clearly.

1 mark — Clear position stated up front and held throughout.

1 mark — At least THREE different persuasive techniques used and identifiable, AND each technique fits naturally into the argument (not forced).

1 mark — At least ONE specific piece of supporting evidence — a credible-sounding fact, statistic, study, or expert quote (can be invented). Plus a clear call to action at the end.

1 mark — Overall quality: logical structure, varied sentence types, persuasive register, and the techniques work together to convince the reader.

Examples of good moves:

For 'schools should start later': cite teen sleep science ('Studies from the University of Auckland show teenagers' natural body clocks shift by two hours during puberty'); rhetorical question ('How can you do your best in maths when your brain is still asleep?'); direct address; call to action ('It's time for our Board of Trustees to listen to the science').

For 'phones should be banned in class': statistic ('Research published in 2023 found that students who keep phones in their pockets score on average 11% lower'); repetition ('Every notification is a distraction. Every distraction is a stolen second of learning'); call to action ('Let's lock the phones away during lessons').

Do NOT award full marks if the paragraph is shorter than 5 sentences, has no clear position, or fails to include a call to action.
